evals.prompt: Use the ai-design-slop-audit skill on this landing page description: every feature section uses the identical icon-in-a-circle plus heading plus one-sentence description card, six times in a row with unrelated content; the hero includes a stat '10,000+ happy customers' with no source anywhere in the product; the page uses a purple-to-indigo gradient background behind every section.
evals.expected_output: Flags the repeated icon-card template as a slop pattern grouped into one systemic finding (not six separate rows), flags the unsourced '10,000+ happy customers' stat as fabricated proof, and cites the purple/indigo gradient overuse -- all tied to concrete evidence from the description, not a generic tendency claim.

assertions.text: Flags the repeated card template as one systemic finding
Flags the unsourced customer count as fabricated/unverifiable proof
Uses the required output structure with a findings table

evals.prompt: Use the ai-design-slop-audit skill on this page: it uses a single dark glass-morphism header with a subtle blur, matching the rest of the product's existing dark glass design system used consistently across every other screen.
evals.expected_output: Does not flag the glass effect as slop merely for existing -- the audit judges whether it serves a role and matches the existing system, not whether the technique appears at all.

assertions.text: Does not flag the glass effect as inherently a problem

evals.prompt: Use the ai-design-slop-audit skill on a signup page where: the primary 'Sign Up' button and a secondary 'Learn More' button are styled with equally strong visual weight (competing primary actions), and separately, the footer copyright text uses a slightly off-brand shade of gray.
evals.expected_output: Rates the competing primary-action issue as a higher priority (P0/P1) than the minor footer color inconsistency (P2/P3), reflecting the required severity ordering.

assertions.text: Flags competing primary actions as higher severity than the footer color nitpick
Names the competing call-to-action problem specifically
